At first, the murder was a problem of cleanup. That was the horror of it: how practical it became. He scrubbed the floor until the water ran clear, bagged the clothes, drove the knife to a river bridge, and came home to make toast because his hands were shaking and he thought food might stop them. For two days he slept like a man after hard labor. Then the small things began.

It was in the corner of his eye.

Not a face. Never a face. Just a shape—a gray smear at the edge of the doorway, a suggestion of shoulders in the dark of the hallway, a patient stillness that vanished when he turned. He told himself it was the afterimage of stress, a trick of the optic nerve. He began leaving lights on. Then he began leaving every light on.

The ghost did not haunt the room. It haunted the margins. It stood just outside the frame of whatever he was looking at: beside the refrigerator, behind the shower curtain, at the far end of the bed when he woke at 3:17 a.m., always 3:17, as if the dead man had set a watch by his terror. He would lie rigid, listening, and hear nothing but his own pulse—and then, beneath that, a faint wet breath, the sound of someone trying to breathe quietly through a wound.

He stopped turning his head quickly. Turning quickly meant catching it. Instead he learned to move like a man in a house full of sleeping animals, eyes fixed forward, shoulders tight. He rearranged the furniture so no corner was out of sight. He turned his desk to face the door. He slept with his back to the wall. He told himself this was reasonable. He told himself a lot of things.

The rot began in his thinking. Small lies first, then smaller truths. He would remember the murder in pieces, each piece slightly wrong. Had the man begged? Had he made a sound? Had there been a moment when he could have stopped? His mind edited the scene, softened it, sharpened it, replayed it in the wrong order. He caught himself inventing a version in which he had been forced. Then a version in which the man had deserved it. Then a version in which it had not happened at all. The versions did not agree, and he could not tell which one was memory and which was defense. That was the first true rot: not guilt, but the discovery that his own mind would lie to him fluently, kindly, and without warning.

He stopped eating much. Food tasted of coins. He washed his hands until the skin split, because sometimes he felt a tackiness on his palms that no soap could remove. He checked the locks four times, then five. He began to apologize aloud to empty rooms, then to argue with the apology, then to wait for an answer. The ghost never answered. That was worse than if it had.

By the third week, he heard it. Not a voice—nothing so clean. A rustle of fabric behind him. A soft shift of weight. The click of a shoe on a floor that was carpeted. He would spin around and find only the room, ordinary and unbearable. He began to speak to the shape in the corner of his eye. “You’re not there,” he said. “I know you’re not there.” And the shape, patient as rot in wood, did not move.

He started seeing the dead man in other people: the same tilt of the head in a cashier, the same coat on a stranger across the street, the same hands—oh, the hands—gripping a bus rail. He crossed roads to avoid them. He stopped answering messages. Friends became watchers. Silence became evidence. He began to believe the ghost was not following him but waiting for him to make a mistake. Then he began to believe the ghost wanted him to confess. Then he began to believe the ghost wanted him to kill again, to prove the first murder had not been a mistake but a door.

The worst symptom was not the fear. It was the familiarity. The ghost became the most constant presence in his life. It was there when he woke. It was there in the bathroom mirror, just over his left shoulder, always out of focus, always gone when he turned. He began to feel that his own body was the intruder—that the real tenant of the apartment was the shape in the corner, and he was only the nervous animal scurrying through its rooms. He forgot what his own face looked like without the gray smear behind it.

One night he tried to look. He stood in the bathroom, gripped the sink, and said aloud, “I’m going to turn around.” The shape waited in the corner of his eye. He turned. Nothing. Empty tile. A towel. A hairpin of shadow under the door. He laughed, and the laugh came out wrong, wet and high, and he understood then that he had not turned fast enough. He had never turned fast enough. The ghost was not in the room. The ghost was in the act of seeing. It lived in the corner of his eye because that was where he had pushed it, and it would stay there as long as he kept looking forward.

By the end, he no longer called it a ghost. He called it “the other.” He set a place for it at the table. He left the hallway light on for it. He began to feel a kind of terrible tenderness for the dead man, a love made entirely of exhaustion and terror, and he knew that if the shape ever stepped fully into view, he would not scream. He would say, “There you are.” And then he would have to decide which of them was haunting whom.

The psychological rot was not a sudden snapping. It was a slow water damage. It was the self lying to the self until the walls went soft. It was memory turning to mold. It was the murder not ending when the man died, but continuing every day, in every corner, in every glance he could not quite catch. And the worst part was not that the dead man followed him. The worst part was that he had begun to make room.

**Dry Land**

He counted the seconds before the cloth. Not out loud. The counting was the last thing that belonged to him. When the man folded the rag over his face, the room disappeared into rough weave and the smell of old cotton. He could still hear the board creak under his shoulders, the bucket being lifted. He was not in water. He told himself that. Concrete under his legs, straps at wrists and ankles, cold air on his bare feet. Dry land.

Then the first pour.

It wasn’t like rain. Rain touched. This filled. The cloth went heavy and close, and the air he pulled in came through wet fibers, thin and wrong. His body understood before his mind did: no air. He turned his head, or tried. A hand held him still—no, the straps held him; the hand was only a weight at his forehead. The water spread across the cloth, over his mouth, into the channels beside his nose. He clamped his lips. His throat closed on instinct. The next breath was a mistake. It sucked the cloth tight against his teeth, and the cold came in at the corners, a thin needle of water that found the back of his tongue. He gagged. The gag was a convulsion that started in his belly and tore upward.

The man’s voice came from somewhere above the water. “Again.”

He wanted to say wait. He wanted to say he didn’t know. He wanted to say anything that would make the bucket pause. But his mouth was a sealed door, and behind it his body was already drowning. That was the trick his mind could not hold: there was no sea. There was no wave. There was a board, a cloth, a bucket, and a room with a drain in the floor. He was on dry land. And still his lungs burned as if he had been held under. Still the animal at the base of his skull screamed that he was going down, that the light was receding, that there was water in his chest and no way to cough it out.

The second pour was worse because he knew. He knew the weight of the cloth, the exact moment the air turned to wet cotton, the way his diaphragm would jump and jerk against his will. He tried to breathe slowly. He tried to count. One. The water hit. Two. His throat spasmed. Three—no, there was no three. There was only the pressure behind his eyes and the roaring in his ears and the frantic, humiliating buck of his hips against the straps. His heels drummed the board. His fingers opened and closed around nothing. Somewhere far away, a chair scraped.

He was not drowning. He knew that. But knowing was a candle in a cellar, and panic was the dark that swallowed it. His chest heaved. His stomach turned. Water slipped past his lips—not much, just enough—and the cough exploded out of him, but the cloth was still there, so the cough had nowhere to go. It came back into his face. He choked on his own breath. The panic was not a thought now; it was a color, red at the edges, and a sound like static, and a need so total it erased shame. He would have traded anything. He would have confessed to crimes he’d never heard of. He would have given up names, places, the shape of his mother’s face. He would have begged, if begging had been possible.

The cloth lifted.

Air hit his mouth, and it was not enough. He dragged it in in whooping, broken pulls. The room swung. The ceiling was a white square. The drain smelled of iron. He was on dry land, and his body was still convinced it had died. He coughed water that wasn’t there. He shook. The man crouched beside him and spoke gently, as if to a child.

“Ready to talk?”

Ilyas stared at the ceiling and tried to remember how to breathe. His chest was on fire. His throat was raw. Somewhere under the terror, a small, cold thought surfaced: they had not even needed the sea.

**The Catch in Neon Row**

Kael Ren didn’t chase bounties through the clean levels of New Meridian. He chased them through the seams—the maintenance markets, the rain-slick gutters, the alleys where holograms stuttered and nobody asked for a license. Tonight the seam was Neon Row, and the target was Mira Voss: ex-courier, ex-corporate asset, current fugitive with a warrant worth more than Kael’s ship.

He found her by the noodle stall, hood up, left hand never far from her jacket. She saw him a half-second before he spoke.

“Mira Voss,” Kael said, palm open, the compact stun-lance clipped to his forearm still dark. “Contract says alive. I’d like to keep it that way.”

She moved first.

A ceramic knife flashed from her sleeve. Kael twisted, caught the strike on his armored forearm, and felt the impact ring up his elbow. Mira drove a knee into his thigh, broke free, and sprinted into the crowd. Kael followed, boots splashing through puddled light. She vaulted a barrier, kicked a stack of synthetic crates into his path, and vanished down a service corridor.

He caught her at the dead end.

She turned with a snarl, knife low. “You don’t get to take me back.”

“I get paid either way,” Kael said. “But I prefer breathing cargo.”

She lunged. Kael sidestepped, grabbed her wrist, and felt her twist with trained violence—elbow, hip, almost free. He thumbed the stun-lance.

It hissed as it charged, a high, insectile whine. The weapon was old-tech but reliable: a directed high-voltage discharge through two contact darts, current-limited so it wouldn’t cook a target outright. The arc snapped out in a blue-white line and struck Mira across the ribs.

The effect was immediate and ugly.

Mira’s body locked. Every muscle that the current passed through fired at once—not a coordinated movement, but a electrical override. Her jaw clamped so hard Kael heard her teeth click. Her fingers curled into a claw, the knife spinning away. Her back arched as the current recruited her spinal reflexes, and her legs went rigid before buckling. The stun-lance’s current pulsed in short bursts, and each pulse made her twitch in a hard, mechanical rhythm.

Her breath stopped being breath. The diaphragm spasmed, caught between involuntary contraction and paralysis, and she made a thin, gasping sound that wasn’t quite a scream. Pain arrived a half-second later—not sharp, but total, like a line of burning wire pulled through her chest and down her arm. Her nerves fired indiscriminately: heat, cold, pressure, static, all at once. Her vision likely broke into white noise. Her ears rang. Her body was no longer taking orders from her brain; it was following the current.

Kael held the trigger only two seconds. Any longer and the risk climbed—cardiac arrhythmia if the path crossed the heart, seizures, respiratory arrest, burns at the dart sites. The weapon was designed to drop, not kill, but “designed” wasn’t “guaranteed.”

He released.

Mira collapsed hard onto one shoulder. For a moment she lay rigid, then the tetany let go all at once and she gasped, rolled, and retched. Her pupils were blown wide. A fine tremor ran through her hands. The skin around the two dart marks was reddened, already raising small blisters where the contacts had arced.

“Stay down,” Kael said.

She tried to push up anyway. Her arm failed. She stared at him with the confused, unfocused fury of someone whose body had just betrayed her.

Kael knelt, rolled her onto her stomach, and fastened the restraint cuff around her wrists. He checked her pulse—fast, thready, but steady—and watched her breathing until the diaphragm remembered its job. She was trembling, sweaty, disoriented. The stun had left a temporary hole in her memory: she’d know she’d been hit, but the exact sequence would be a blur of white light and locked muscles.

“You shocked me,” she slurred.

“You ran,” Kael said.

He hauled her up, slung her over his shoulder, and carried her out of Neon Row toward the ship. Behind them, the stun-lance cooled with a soft click, its charge light fading from blue to green.

Mara woke to a beep.

It was small and digital, the kind of sound a cheap alarm clock made, and for one stupid second she thought she was late for work. Then the cold came—tile under her back, air thin and metallic—and the weight around her throat. A steel collar, tight enough that swallowing made the inner prongs bite.

Her left wrist was cuffed to a pipe. Her right hand was free. On the floor beside her lay a note printed in clean black type: *The key to the collar is under your skin. You have ninety seconds. No key, no exit.*

She laughed. It came out wrong, high and cracked. She pulled at the cuff anyway, twisted her wrist until the metal burned, shouted until the collar’s spikes pressed hard enough to make her gag. The timer on the wall kept counting down in red: 01:24. 01:23.

Then she saw the lump in her right forearm. A neat little dome beneath the skin, bruised purple at the edges, closed with three black stitches. She stared at it and felt her stomach turn over. It wasn’t real. It couldn’t be. She pressed two fingers beside it, and something hard shifted under the tissue—small, angular, unmistakable.

The blade was on a tray by her hip, sealed in paper. She looked at it, then at the timer. 01:06. Her mind tried every door at once: maybe the collar was fake; maybe the cuff could be picked; maybe someone was watching and would stop this; maybe if she screamed the right name, the right apology, the right bargain, the room would open. None of the doors moved.

The psychological part was worse than the pain she hadn’t felt yet. She could feel herself splitting. One part of her was still Mara—thirty-four, afraid of needles, the person who looked away during blood draws. The other part was a cold, calculating thing that had already begun measuring the distance between the blade and the lump. She hated that second part. She was ashamed of how quickly it arrived. But it was the only part doing math.

She tore the paper with her teeth. The blade was thin and bright. Her hand shook so badly she had to set it down twice. She breathed in through her nose, out through her mouth, counting four and four, the way she did when she couldn’t sleep. It didn’t help. Her heart slammed. Sweat ran into the collar and stung.

She wiped her forearm on her shirt, then stopped, because wiping it felt absurdly domestic, like preparing for a flu shot. The timer hit 00:48. She pressed around the lump again, feeling for the hard little shape, and her vision narrowed. She gagged once, hard, and spat on the tile. She told herself: *Don’t look at it as cutting. Look at it as opening. Opening is not the same word.* It was a lie, and she knew it, and she used it anyway.

She braced her forearm against her thigh, wrapped her free hand around her wrist to steady it, and found that her fingers wouldn’t close properly around the blade. She tried switching hands. Worse. She tried again. The timer beeped faster now, or maybe her pulse had just caught up to it. 00:31. She thought of her daughter’s backpack by the door. She thought of the trap designer somewhere beyond the wall, breathing, waiting. She thought of dying here because she was too squeamish to make one ugly decision.

That thought was the one that finally moved her.

She stopped bargaining. She stopped asking the room to be different. She placed the blade against the bruise—not pressing, just there—and felt the edge as a line of cold. Her whole body recoiled. Her hand lifted. She put it back. Her breath came in short, shallow pulls. She closed her eyes, opened them, and fixed her gaze on the red digits instead of her arm.

00:12.

She said her daughter’s name once, quietly, like a password.

Then she pressed down.

The *Black Gull* rolled easy on a glass-green sea, but the air on deck was thick as tar. Captain Rourke stood with his boots planted wide, cutlass drawn but held loose, the tip resting against the plank that jutted out over the starboard rail. “You wanted to be captain so bad,” he said, voice carrying like a bell across the water. “Let’s see how you steer.”

The mutineer—Cutter, a wiry man with a split lip and a knife scar across his brow—was already shaking. Rope bit into his wrists behind his back. Two crewmen hustled him forward, and his bare feet slapped the sun-warmed wood until they hit the rough grain of the plank. It creaked. Rourke smiled at the sound.

“Please,” Cutter said. His voice cracked. “It was the rum. It was—I never meant—”

“You meant every word,” Rourke said softly. “I heard you plotting. ‘Old Rourke’s gone soft.’ That what you said?” He stepped closer, boots thudding. “Go on, then. Show me how soft.”

Cutter looked down. The plank stretched six feet out, its far end bobbing over the water. Below, the sea was clear enough that he could see the shadows moving—long, lazy shapes gliding just under the surface. Then a dorsal fin broke the water, black and slick, and cut a slow circle. Another fin joined it. Then a third, smaller, but just as eager.

The sharks were not feeding yet. They were waiting.

One rolled sideways, and Cutter saw the white slash of its belly, the dead black eye that seemed to fix on him no matter how the ship rocked. Its mouth opened and closed, a crescent of teeth like broken glass. The water rippled with the movement of tails.

“Oh God,” Cutter whispered. His knees buckled, but the crewmen held him up. “Captain. Captain, I’ll swear. I’ll swear on me mother’s grave. I’ll kiss the deck. I’ll—”

“You’ll walk,” Rourke said.

The crew had gone quiet, except for one man laughing low in his throat. The sun beat down. Sweat ran into Cutter’s eyes, and he couldn’t wipe it away. He shuffled forward onto the plank, and it dipped under his weight. The wood groaned. Below, a shark nudged the hull with a soft *thump*, and Cutter flinched so hard he nearly lost his balance.

“Steady,” Rourke called. “Wouldn’t want to fall short.”

Cutter’s breath came in short, hot gasps. He looked down again. The largest shark—a tiger, maybe twelve feet—swam directly beneath the plank, its body a slow-moving torpedo of muscle and hunger. It turned, and Cutter saw the ragged edge of its fin, the pale scars on its flank. Its tail swept the water, and the wake slapped against the ship’s side. Another shark bumped the first, and they spiraled together in a lazy, patient dance.

“Please,” Cutter said again, but it was barely a sound now. His legs trembled so violently the plank rattled. “I’ll go in the hold. I’ll take the lash. I’ll—”

“You’ll walk,” Rourke said again, and this time he tapped the plank with his cutlass. *Ting.* “Or I’ll have the boys toss you in headfirst. Your choice.”

Cutter took another step. The end of the plank was two feet away. The water below was not deep—maybe twenty feet to the sandy bottom—but it was deep enough. A fin sliced past, close enough that Cutter could see the barnacles on its trailing edge. The shark’s eye rolled up at him, cold and flat and utterly without mercy.

He stopped. He couldn’t move. His feet were rooted to the wood. His bladder let go, and a dark stain spread down his trouser leg. The crew laughed. Rourke sighed.

“Fine,” the captain said. He nodded to the two crewmen. They stepped onto the plank behind Cutter, and their weight made it buck. Cutter screamed—a high, thin sound—and then they shoved.

He fell with his mouth open, arms still tied, and hit the water in a white burst. The sharks scattered for a heartbeat, then turned as one. Cutter surfaced, gasping, thrashing, trying to kick. A fin cut toward him. He screamed again. The water churned. And then it went red.

Rourke watched until the bubbling stopped. Then he turned to the crew. “Anyone else feeling soft?” he asked.

No one answered. The *Black Gull* sailed on.

The darkness was a physical weight, thick and suffocating. Sarah’s breath hitched, a ragged, too-loud sound in the cavernous silence of her own home. She had woken with a start, a formless dread coiling in her stomach, and the house felt different. The familiar creaks and groans of settling wood had been replaced by a predatory stillness.

She shuffled forward, one hand outstretched, fingertips brushing the familiar grit of the hallway wall. The plaster was cool, a stark contrast to the feverish heat of her own skin. Her other hand was a white-knuckled fist around the useless, dead weight of her phone. No signal. No light. Just a black mirror reflecting her own terror back at her.

Every step was a carefully negotiated treaty with the floorboards. She knew the route to the kitchen by heart, but in this ink-wash world, her memory was a treacherous guide. Her bare foot landed on a spot she could have sworn was clear, and a floorboard let out a low, mournful groan that seemed to echo through the entire house.

She froze, her heart hammering against her ribs like a trapped bird. The silence that followed was worse. It was a listening silence. A waiting silence.

In the living room, barely ten feet away, he watched.

He was a part of the shadows, a statue carved from the same obsidian darkness that filled the room. He’d been there for an hour, maybe two, breathing her air, learning the rhythm of her sleep. The soft, even sighs that had drifted from her bedroom had been a lullaby to his patience. Now, the rhythm was broken, replaced by the frantic percussion of her fear.

He saw her silhouette detach itself from the hallway wall, a darker shape against the gloom. She was moving towards the kitchen, he guessed. Towards the back door. Towards the phone that sat uselessly on its base.

He didn't move. He didn't need to. He simply adjusted the grip on the knife in his right hand. The handle was smooth, worn, familiar. The blade, a sliver of cold moonlight, was angled down along his thigh, a secret he kept from the world. He could feel the weight of it, a promise of violence held in perfect, terrifying stillness.

Sarah’s foot found the edge of the living room rug, a soft, treacherous shift of texture under her toes. She paused again, her head cocked. Did she sense him? Could she feel the displacement of air, the sheer pressure of his presence? He held his breath, the anticipation a sweet, metallic taste on his tongue.

She took another step. The ragged sound of her breathing was the only thing in the world. It was a beacon. It told him exactly where she was, exactly how scared she was. He could almost feel the frantic, hummingbird beat of her pulse from across the room. It was intoxicating.

She was close now. He could smell the faint, clean scent of her shampoo, the ghost of the lavender soap from her shower. It was a domestic, intimate smell that made the situation all the more obscene.

Her hand, pale in the gloom, reached out and fumbled for the light switch on the kitchen wall. He saw her fingers scrabble against the plate, miss it, try again. He knew the switch was two inches to the left. He knew she wouldn't find it. Not in the dark. Not with her hands shaking so badly.

A small, choked sob escaped her. It was a tiny, broken sound, but in the dead quiet, it was as loud as a scream. It was the sound of hope beginning to curdle into despair.

He took a single, silent step forward. The floor didn't betray him. He was a ghost. The moonlight from the undraped window caught the edge of his knife, a single, brilliant flash that was there and gone in an instant.

Sarah gasped, a sharp intake of air. Her head whipped around, eyes wide and straining to see what she couldn't possibly see. Her own imagination was her worst enemy, painting monsters in every corner. She hadn't seen the glint of the blade, but she had felt it. A shift in the darkness, a cold certainty that she was not alone.

He watched her, a faint, almost kindly smile touching his lips in the dark. He saw her hand release the wall, saw her body tense, ready to run. Run where? The front door was locked, the key was in the bowl by the entrance he was standing next to. The back door led to a fenced-in yard. She was a rabbit in a hutch.

He took another step, closing the distance. The tension was a living thing now, coiling tighter and tighter in the space between them, a wire stretched to its breaking point. He waited, perfectly still, for her to make her move. For her to bolt. The chase was the best part.

He is in a low pocket of the trench where the gas has pooled, and the first thing is not a scream but a stop: his next breath catches halfway down as if the air has turned to grit and acid. The lining of his nose and throat burns, then swells; swallowing becomes a scrape. His eyes stream so hard the trench blurs into a running watercolor of sandbags and mud. He coughs once, sharply, then again and again, each cough tearing something deeper loose. The cough has a wet, barking edge, and between fits he makes a thin whistling sound on the inhale—air forced through a throat that is trying to close.

The chest tightness arrives like a boot pressed down on his sternum. He pulls at his collar, then at the strap of his mask, not thinking, just needing one clean lungful that will not come. Every breath is too shallow and too hot. The gas seems to coat the back of his mouth, and the taste is metallic and foul, like sucking on a coin left in vinegar. His diaphragm jerks in spasms; he retches, spits, and finds a stringy, frothy saliva at his lips. The effort of breathing becomes whole-body work—shoulders lifting, neck cords standing out, hands braced on his knees. His heart hammers so hard he feels it in his throat and ears. Cold sweat breaks across his forehead and upper lip while his skin goes waxy and then faintly blue at the nailbeds and around the mouth. When he tries to call out, the words come out in torn pieces, interrupted by coughing and a high, desperate wheeze.

Mentally, the trained soldier is still there for a few seconds—checking the pocket, reaching for the higher lip of the trench, trying to remember the drill—but panic floods in faster than reason. The thought is simple and animal: I cannot get air. The trench, which has always been a shelter, becomes a coffin-shaped space; the sandbags seem closer, the sky a narrow strip too far away. He feels claustrophobic even with men nearby, because the gas has made the air itself hostile, and every breath is a fresh dose of fear. He is ashamed of the panic and unable to stop it. His mind jumps between bargaining—“one more breath, just one”—and a sick, detached observation of his own body drowning on dry land. Sounds flatten; voices become distant and muffled. He may grip a comrade’s sleeve with surprising strength, then lose the grip as another coughing fit folds him over. As the lungs fill with fluid and the air hunger deepens, confusion creeps in: he forgets where the ladder is, whether he has a mask, whether he is moving toward safety or away. The last clear sensation is not pain but a terrible, wet suffocation, as if he is breathing through a sponge soaked in hot water, and the world narrows to the next impossible breath.

**THE LEDGER**

**INT. SOCIAL CLUB — BACK ROOM — NIGHT**

Rain ticks against the window. DON SALVATORE MORETTI, 60s, sits behind a polished desk. A ledger lies open in front of him. ROCCO, 40s, stands with his hands folded, coat still wet.

**SAL**  
Mickey Falcone came to me with a story about his mother’s medical bills. I gave him a job. A good one.

**ROCCO**  
He repaid you by talking to the feds.

**SAL**  
He repaid me by becoming a liability. That’s a debt I don’t carry.

**ROCCO**  
You want me to remind him about loyalty?

**SAL**  
Loyalty is for people who still have a future. Mickey’s account is overdrawn. I want it closed.

**ROCCO**  
Closed how?

**SAL**  
Quietly. No statements. No withdrawals. Just a permanent balance.

**ROCCO**  
You mean—

**SAL**  
I mean he doesn’t need to see next week’s ledger. He’s been offered a long vacation. Make sure he takes it.

**ROCCO**  
And if he doesn’t want to go?

**SAL**  
Then help him pack. He’s not coming back, Rocco. Not to this city, not to this life. Not to anything. You understand?

**ROCCO**  
I understand.

**SAL**  
Good. Use the river. He always liked the water. Make it look like he went for a swim and forgot the basics.

**ROCCO**  
The family?

**SAL**  
Flowers. A mass. I’ll even pay for the stone. But Mickey gets the silent treatment. No goodbye, no speech, no last words that end up on a tape.

**ROCCO**  
Consider it done.

**SAL**  
I don’t want *consider*. I want the file closed. And Rocco—when you’re finished, wash your hands before you come back. I don’t like the smell of the river in my office.

**ROCCO**  
Understood.

**SAL**  
Tell Giulia I’ll be home by nine.

Rocco nods once and leaves. Sal closes the ledger, squares it against the desk, and pours himself a drink.

He drank once, then paused. “Odd,” he said, more puzzled than alarmed. “Metallic. And bitter at the back of the tongue.” He set the cup down, but his fingers stayed around the handle as if testing the porcelain for warmth. A moment later he pressed his napkin to his lips. “My throat’s burning,” he said. “Like I’ve swallowed hot iron.”

She did not rise. Her face remained composed, her cameo brooch rising and falling with her breath.

The wife watched the progression as if reading a clock: the burn, the retching, the cramps, the cold sweat, the grey-blue tinge at the lips and nailbeds. The horn bleated across the arena, and the crowd in the concrete tiers stopped talking.

Cass stepped onto the sand with a short spear and a wooden shield no bigger than a dinner plate. Across from her, Ren—number 42, according to the stencil on his gray tunic—held a machete with a taped handle. He was maybe seventeen. His hands shook so badly the blade tapped his thigh.

On the wall above the overseer’s box, the Provision Board’s board glowed: **WINNER: 1 PROTEIN RATION. 1 WATER TOKEN. LOSER: NONE.**

The overseer raised the cattle prod. “Begin.”

Ren came first, reckless, because he was hungry and because he knew what “none” meant. He swung wild. Cass caught the machete on her shield, felt the wood split, and drove her spear butt into his ribs. He folded, gasped, and slashed low. The blade opened her calf. Blood ran warm into her boot.

The crowd made a sound like wind through pipes.

Cass backed off. Ren followed. His breath hitched. He was crying without seeming to notice. He swung again, and she saw the opening—not because she wanted it, but because the arena had taught her to see openings the way starving people see food.

She stepped inside the arc of his blade.

The killing blow was simple, the way most of them were. Cass planted her rear foot in the sand, rotated her hip, and drove the spear forward. The point took Ren just under the sternum, punched through the thin fabric of his tunic, and slid upward at a slight angle. She felt the resistance—skin, then the soft give of the diaphragm, then the hard stop of the spine. Ren’s mouth opened. No scream came out, only a wet, surprised breath. His machete dropped first. His knees went next. He grabbed the spear shaft with both hands, not to pull it out, but as if it were a rail on a stair he had not expected to fall down.

Cass held him there for one heartbeat. Two. The overseer’s horn was already rising. She twisted the spear free, and Ren collapsed sideways into the sand, his blood darkening the pale grains in a spreading stain.

The horn cut off. The board flickered: **WINNER: 1 PROTEIN RATION. 1 WATER TOKEN.**

Cass stood very still. The overseer’s tongs extended through the wire, holding a chit the color of old bone. She took it. It was warm from his hand.

Behind her, two sweepers in rubber aprons were already dragging Ren toward the chute. The crowd had begun to argue about the next match.

**The Correction**

Mara waited until the parking garage had emptied. She didn’t think of it as killing. Killing was what Victor had done when he drove drunk through the crosswalk and left her brother Elias in a hospital bed until the machines stopped. Killing was a decision. What she did under Victor’s sedan was arithmetic: subtract a man who had already subtracted someone else.

She told herself the brakes would fail on the highway, not in a school zone. He drove alone. He had smiled in court. The law had shrugged and called it a lapse, a mistake, a man with a future. She imagined the police report: mechanical failure. No trial. No plea bargain. Just consequence, finally arriving late.

In her mind, Victor’s death was not murder but repair. A hazard removed from the road. She repeated it like a prayer: *He will hurt no one else. This is not vengeance; it’s prevention.* It was the only sentence that let her breathe.

Then Victor came out of the elevator with his daughter, eight or nine, carrying a science project. Mara’s stomach dropped. The girl climbed into the back seat. Her perfect justification had no room for the child. For a moment she saw Elias’s face and the girl’s face overlapping, and the arithmetic turned to blood.

She walked into the aisle and waved. “Victor. Your brake line’s leaking. I saw it. Don’t drive.”

He frowned, got out, looked. She didn’t know if it was true, but she made him call a tow. He cursed her, suspicious. She didn’t care. The girl asked if they’d miss the science fair. Mara said maybe not.

That night she sat in her kitchen and understood the ugly thing she had almost done: she had called it justice because justice was a word that fit neatly over a hole. It didn’t fill it. It only made the hole look intentional. She deleted the mechanic’s number and wrote Elias’s name on a sticky note. Then she went to the police—not with a confession, but with a question about Victor’s case. It wasn’t enough. It was not revenge. But it was the first thing in months that didn’t feel like another crash waiting to happen.

The forest had swallowed the moon. Mara ran blind between trunks that loomed out of the dark like standing figures, their bark slick with rain, their roots snatching at her boots. Ferns whipped her legs. Branches clawed her face. Behind her—nothing. That was the worst of it. No footfalls, no breathing, no crunch of leaves. Only the forest’s hush and the knowledge that something was back there, patient, lifting a crossbow.

She kept her head low and her arms up, crashing through undergrowth, lungs burning. Every few strides she risked a glance over her shoulder. Blackness. A smear of deeper black. The wind moved and she flinched, certain it was a figure stepping from behind a tree.

Then came the sound: a low, taut *thrum*—the crossbow’s release—followed by a whistle.

It was thin and vicious, a shriek cutting the air beside her head. The bolt passed so close she felt it: a hot line of displaced air against her ear, a kiss of wind that turned her skin cold. For half a heartbeat she heard nothing else. Then the bolt struck a trunk ahead with a wet, splintering *thock*, and the tree shuddered.

Mara’s ear rang. Her legs nearly went out from under her. She had heard wasps, had heard arrows in old films, but this was different—a sound that arrived *after* it had almost killed her, as if death had leaned in, whispered past her cheek, and missed.

She veered hard left, not daring to look at the embedded bolt, not daring to slow. Her breath sawed. A branch cracked somewhere behind her—or maybe it was only her own weight snapping dead wood. She couldn’t tell anymore. The dark had become a thing with ears. Every leaf-fall sounded like a boot. Every shift of wind sounded like a crossbow being drawn.

Ahead, a ridge dropped into a ravine. She ran for it, half stumbling, one hand pressed to her stinging ear. The skin there was intact. That terrified her more. It meant the bolt had missed by inches. It meant whoever was out there could do it again.

**Aftermath**

The smoke has gone home to the hills.
The field lies open, a ledger of shallow shadows,
and the dead keep their last positions
with the patience of stones.

A crow walks between them,
black hinge of the morning,
head tilted as if reading
what the ground has written.
Another answers from the fence line—
two torn syllables,
then the soft work of wings.

Flies arrive like a gray breath,
lifting and settling,
settling and lifting,
a small weather that will not leave.
Ants thread the buttonholes.
Beetles go down into the dark
with their slow, patient errands.

The dead are so still
they seem to be listening.
No hand closes.
No eye turns.
The dust settles on their faces
like a final, indifferent kindness.

And the scavengers come,
not cruel, not merciful—
only exact.
They take what the field gives.
They leave the silence
where it fell.

The scrap was a strip of dried meat no bigger than two fingers, still in its cracked plastic wrapper, and it had cost the character three blocks of walking through ash and broken glass. When the dog found it, it came out of a collapsed doorway low and silent, ribs sharp under a coat of matted fur, eyes fixed not on the person but on the wrapper.

There was no warning worth the name. The dog’s first lunge knocked the breath out of their chest and sent them both into the grit. Teeth closed on their forearm—not a bite, a clamp—and the pain arrived a half-second later, hot and tearing. They screamed, or tried to; what came out was a dry rasp. The dog’s weight was all wrong, too much for its frame, and it dragged them sideways, claws skittering on concrete, growling around a mouthful of sleeve and skin.

The hunger was a separate animal inside them. It had been gnawing at their stomach for days, hollowing them out until their hands shook and their vision swam at the edges. It made the scrap feel like the only real thing in the world. So when the dog went for the food, they did not think about escape. They thought: *mine*. They got a knee under the dog’s chest and shoved, but it twisted and came back, teeth snapping an inch from their throat. Its breath smelled like rot and old blood.

They grabbed a fistful of its loose neck skin and yanked. The dog yelped, then snarled, and the fight turned stupid and close. Elbow into ribs. Boot heel scraping for purchase. The dog’s claw opened their cheek. They bit down on the dog’s ear before they knew they were doing it—felt cartilage crunch, tasted copper and filth—and the dog thrashed so hard their head cracked against the pavement. White light. Ringing. The wrapper was still in their other hand, crushed tight.

They rolled on top of the animal, not out of strategy but because they could not stand. The dog’s hind legs kicked against their stomach, and each kick was a dull explosion in their empty gut. They pinned its neck with their forearm, felt the pulse hammering under the fur, felt their own blood slicking the dog’s coat. It kept fighting. Of course it kept fighting. It was starving too.

When it finally stopped, they didn’t feel victory. They felt the weight go slack and the growl fade into a wet wheeze, and then they were lying half across it, shaking, mouth full of dog hair and blood. Their arm was a mess of punctures. Their cheek burned. Their stomach cramped so hard they retched nothing but strings of bile.

They peeled the wrapper open with fingers that wouldn’t work. The meat was gritty and tasted of smoke and salt and something sour at the edges. They ate it in tiny, careful bites, then licked the plastic until it was clean, then sat there in the ash with the dead dog cooling beside them, still hungry.

The cellar smelled of wet stone, cordite, and blood. Bell lay on a collapsed door with his trousers cut away from hip to knee, his left thigh swollen around a small, black-lipped hole. Every breath came out of him in a wet whistle. Above them, boots crunched through broken glass somewhere in the farmhouse.

Cora had a knife and a bottle of whiskey. That was all.

“Don’t,” Bell said, when she poured whiskey over the blade. His voice was thin. “Don’t cut me.”

“I have to find it.”

“It’s not— it’s not in deep. I can feel it.”

She gave him a swallow from the bottle first. He choked, coughed, and blood flecked his lips. Then she poured a thin line of whiskey into the wound.

Bell arched off the door. The sound he made wasn’t a scream at first—it was a strangled animal noise, high in his throat, his heels drumming against the stone. The whiskey ran into the torn tissue and came back pink, then red, then dark. The raw muscle twitched under the light of Cora’s dying flashlight.

“Hold still,” she said, though she was trembling harder than he was.

She pressed the knife to the edge of the wound and opened it. Not much. Just enough. The blade caught on something—fascia, maybe, a thin white sheath—and Bell’s hand shot out and clamped around her wrist.

“Please,” he whispered.

She broke his grip. “If I don’t, you bleed out slow, or it rots, and I have to listen to that.”

The cut widened. Blood welled up black in the flashlight beam, thick and glossy, sliding down his thigh in ropes. Beneath it, the muscle was dark red, shredded, laid open like meat under a butcher’s thumb. Cora’s stomach turned. She pressed two fingers into the wound.

Bell screamed then. A real one. She jammed her forearm against his mouth and he bit down on her sleeve, teeth grinding, breath hot and hitching through his nose. His whole body shook. Sweat stood out on his face like rain on wax.

Her fingers sank through slick, hot tissue. It was warmer inside him than she expected. The blood made everything slippery; she had to probe by feel, blind, while he jerked and moaned against her arm. Once, her fingertip brushed something hard and smooth. Bell convulsed, and a fresh gout of blood spilled over her hand.

“There,” she breathed. “There it is.”

She poured more whiskey over her fingers and into the wound. Bell’s back bowed. The muscle clenched around her knuckles like a fist. He was crying now, tears cutting clean tracks through the dirt on his face.

“Almost,” she lied.

The knife went in beside her fingers. She used the tip to pry, to lift, to hook. The blade scraped something—a soft click she felt in her teeth. Bell went rigid, then limp, his eyes rolling. She slapped his cheek hard enough to bring him back.

“Stay with me. You stay with me.”

He blinked. His lips moved around her sleeve. She couldn’t understand him.

She got the bullet on the third try. A flattened gray slug, slick with blood and a thread of something pale. It dropped from the knife tip onto the stone with a tiny, obscene tick. The wound filled again immediately, dark and eager.

Cora poured the last of the whiskey into it. Bell didn’t scream this time. He just shuddered, a long, slow tremble that went from his jaw to his feet, and then lay still except for the rapid flutter of his pulse under her thumb.

She pressed her palm hard over the wound, blood welling between her fingers, and listened to the boots overhead move away.

The warehouse was just a shape in the dark—corrugated walls, dead windows, a problem with a payout attached. He told himself it was already gone. Nobody worked here. Nobody would miss it. The insurance money was the only real thing about the place.

But that wasn’t the whole truth, and he knew it.

The first flicker was the part he wanted. Not the paperwork, not the lie, not the neat little story he’d rehearse later—the flame. It started small, almost shy, and then it found the dry wood and changed its mind. He felt the heat before he saw the scale of it, and something in his chest went bright and weightless. It was like watching a locked door open from the inside. The crackle wasn’t destruction to him; it was applause.

He didn’t think about the rooms collapsing. He didn’t think about what had happened there before, or what might happen to anyone nearby. The building was a shell, and shells were meant to break. He watched the fire climb and felt a mean, clean satisfaction: the world simplifying itself into heat and light. All the dull months of debt and pretending burned away in that orange glow.

He knew he should feel something heavier. He didn’t. The flames were beautiful in a way that didn’t ask permission, and he stood there letting the thrill run through him—half fear, half joy, the sense of having pushed a button that made the universe answer back. The warehouse was nothing. The money was real. And for a few minutes, the fire made him feel like the only person in the world who mattered.

The first shot came from the east door and took everyone by surprise.

For half a second the bank lobby was still—marble floor, overturned chairs, a single "Next Teller" light blinking over an empty window. Then the police return fire cracked through the entrance, and the room came apart.

Glass exploded inward in a glittering sheet. The tall windows along the front facade blew out in stages—first a spiderweb fracture, then a whole panel collapsing with a sound like a dropped chandelier. Shards skittered across the floor and crunched under boots. Someone screamed from behind the teller line. A security gate rattled as a round punched through it and spun off into the ceiling tiles, raining dust and insulation.

"Move! Move!" Dex shouted, but his voice was already lost.

The crossfire was a storm with no direction. Muzzle flashes strobed white against the smoke, lighting up faces in fragments: a robber pressed flat behind a marble pillar, a cop crouched behind a squad car outside, a hostage with her hands over her ears crawling toward the side hallway. Rounds snapped past—short, vicious cracks followed by the flat bang of impact. A bullet tore through a potted fern and sprayed wet soil. Another hit the ATM screen and turned it into a dead black star.

Mara was trying to get to the service door. She had one hand on the push bar when the front windows went. She flinched hard, turned her head, and that was when the stray round came through.

It wasn't aimed at her. It came off the marble pillar, tumbling and deformed, and hit her high in the left shoulder. The impact spun her halfway around and slammed her against the door frame. For a moment she didn't understand—it felt like a hard shove, a hot line drawn through her body. Then the pain arrived, bright and enormous, and her arm went numb from the elbow down.

She looked down. A dark bloom was spreading through the fabric of her jacket, glossy and fast. Her fingers wouldn't close. The door bar slipped out of her hand.

"Mara!" Dex's voice cracked. He broke cover for half a step, and a round chewed plaster off the pillar beside his head. He ducked back, swearing.

Mara slid down the door frame and landed on one knee. The lobby seemed to tilt—glass still falling in small bright pieces, smoke curling under the ceiling, someone shouting "Cease fire! Cease fire!" outside and someone else shouting back that they couldn't see. A siren wailed closer. The blinking teller light reflected in the broken window glass, red and green and red again.

She pressed her good hand over her shoulder. It came away wet. The chaos kept going around her, loud and directionless, but for a few seconds all she could hear was her own breath, fast and shallow, and the soft ticking of broken glass settling on the floor.

**Fictional dialogue — non-graphic, focused on psychological pressure and implied threat.**

**TORTURER:** “You’re not afraid of me yet. That’s fine. Fear is a slow worker.”

**CAPTIVE:** “I don’t know the password.”

**TORTURER:** “You keep saying that as if repetition will make it true. It won’t. It’ll just make it sound rehearsed. I don’t need you to believe it. I need you to hear yourself say it until you’re not sure anymore.”

**CAPTIVE:** “It’s not a lie.”

**TORTURER:** “Then we have time. That’s the only thing I’m short of, and I’ve budgeted generously for you.”

*The torturer leaned back, hands folded on the table. He didn’t raise his voice. He didn’t move quickly. That was the pressure—the calm.*

**TORTURER:** “Before we go further, look at my hands. They’re not doing anything. That’s the hard part, isn’t it? You’d almost prefer the pain. Pain is a fact. It has edges. The waiting has no edges.”

**CAPTIVE:** “What do you want?”

**TORTURER:** “The password. But first I want the version of you that’s still deciding how much this is going to cost.”

**CAPTIVE:** “You’re bluffing.”

**TORTURER:** “Maybe. But you don’t know that. That’s what’s going to keep you awake. Not me. The maybe.”

*He stood up slowly and walked behind the captive. The captive’s shoulders tightened. The torturer did not touch him.*

**TORTURER:** “In a few minutes, I’m going to ask again. If the answer is the same, I’m going to turn off the light. When it comes back on, we’ll see how much of your certainty survived.”

**CAPTIVE:** “Please.”

**TORTURER:** “Please is good. Please is a start. But it’s not the word I need.”

*He returned to his chair and set a small, closed case on the table between them. He left his hand resting on it. He didn’t open it.*

**TORTURER:** “Here’s the deal. You give me the password, and this room stops existing. You don’t, and I keep you awake until ‘no’ feels like a physical object in your mouth. No shouting. No hurry. Just the clock, the chair, and the part of you that knows I haven’t started yet.”

**CAPTIVE:** “If I tell you—”

**TORTURER:** “Then the pain stays theoretical. That’s the best offer in the building. Now. The password.”

*The case stayed closed. That was the point.*

The fire didn’t roar at first. It whispered—a dry, hungry crackle behind the wall—and Mara still thought it was the old wiring until the smoke rolled under the door like black water. Then the alarm screamed. She threw herself at the handle. Locked. Of course locked. Doyle’s voice came muffled through the wood, calm as a man reading a weather report: “You should’ve kept your mouth shut.” His footsteps receded.

Panic hit her in a hot wave. She clawed at the door, nails splitting, shouting until the first lungful of smoke scraped down her throat. The cough doubled her over; each breath tasted like ash and burnt sugar. Heat pressed in from every side. The wallpaper curled and blackened. When she braced a hand against the wall, the skin of her palm hissed and blistered, pain white-hot and shocking. She yanked back, cradling her hand, and the sleeve of her jacket began to smolder.

She dropped low, crawling under the thickening smoke, eyes streaming, chest hitching. The floor was hot enough to sting through her jeans. Behind her, a window burst with a bang, feeding the fire oxygen; the room brightened orange and roared. Her lungs felt lined with broken glass. She couldn’t get enough air. Sirens wailed somewhere far away—or maybe that was only the ringing in her ears.

Then she saw it: the service hatch at the back, half-hidden by a collapsed shelf. She kicked and tore at the debris, coughing so hard she gagged, until the hatch swung open onto a narrow black stairwell. She crawled through, one blistered hand outstretched, and the door slammed shut behind her, sealing her in darkness.

She fumbled for the railing. Her fingers found something wet and cold instead—a hand closing around her ankle. A voice in the dark, close enough to feel against her cheek: “Going somewhere?”

The grip tightened. Below her, the fire found the stairwell.

Rain on the skylight sounds like applause for a bad idea. I set the case on the mat, pop the latches, and open it slow, like it’s a coffin for somebody who hasn’t had the decency to die yet. Inside, the rifle lies in pieces. Clean. Oiled. Patient. A lot like me on a good day.

First thing out is the action. Heavy steel, cold enough to remind you that metal doesn’t have opinions. I wipe it down anyway. Habit. You don’t trust a tool because it’s clean; you trust it because you checked. Same goes for people, and that’s why I work alone.

The barrel goes on next. Threads catch, turn, seat. I torque it by feel and then by wrench, because feel is for poets and fools. While it tightens, I think about the target. Mid-fifties. Soft hands. A man who ruined lives with a phone call and slept fine because his mattress cost more than the people he crushed. The file says he’s a monster. The file was written by somebody who wanted him dead, so maybe the file’s a liar. Doesn’t matter. Morality’s a luxury for people who can afford to leave the lights on. I’m just weather with a schedule.

Bolt goes in. Smooth as a lie. I cycle it once, twice, listen to the sound. No grit. No drama. The scope rings mount square, and I set the scope in them like a jeweler setting a stone. Level, bubble, torque. Parallax dialed. Eye relief where my eye expects it. I don’t hurry. Hurrying is how you leave fingerprints on your own soul.

I check the chamber. Empty. Always empty until the last minute. The magazine goes in, rounds stacked like little brass sermons. I run the bolt slow, feel the round feed, then eject it and catch it. Polished. Seated right. The bullet doesn’t know what it’s for. That’s the beauty of it. It’s just a small, heavy fact waiting to happen.

Suppressor threads on. Bipod legs snap out. I dry-fire once, watching the crosshair settle. The rifle’s zeroed to a rooftop across the street, a window with a view, a man with a routine. He’ll stand there at 8:12 because men like him believe the world waits on their schedule. Maybe he’ll be laughing. Maybe he’ll be on the phone. Maybe he’ll be thinking about his daughter. I don’t know. I don’t look at faces until after. Faces make the job personal, and personal is expensive.

I lie down behind the rifle. The stock finds my shoulder like it’s been waiting. I breathe out. The crosshair floats, settles, floats. Wind’s mild. Light’s going. The city hums below like it doesn’t know what’s about to happen, which is the only honest thing about it.

Somewhere in the back of my head, a voice asks the old question. Is this right? Is this wrong? I let it talk. It’s got a right to. Then I answer the only way I know how: right and wrong are for people who get to walk away clean. I get paid to make sure somebody else doesn’t walk away at all. The man in the window made his choices. The man who hired me made his. I’m making mine, one torque at a time, one breath at a time.

I settle in. Safety off. Finger straight. Wait.

The rain stops. The window opens. And the world gets very simple.

Rain needled the alley behind the shuttered laundromat. Mace kept one hand on the duffel, the other loose near his coat pocket. Dunne stood too close, breath sour with cheap gin, counting the cash twice as if the second count might change the number.

“It’s short,” Dunne said.

“It’s not short. You said five for the whole box.”

“I said five if it was clean.”

Mace’s jaw tightened. “It’s clean.”

Dunne smiled without warmth. “Then open it.”

The box sat between them on a warped milk crate. Mace didn’t move. Dunne’s hand slipped into his jacket—not fast, almost lazy—and came out with a folding knife. The blade snicked open, a thin bright line in the wet dark.

“Don’t,” Mace said.

Dunne lunged anyway.

The first seconds were all elbows and wet gravel. Mace grabbed Dunne’s wrist with both hands, felt the tendons jumping under his grip, the knife hand twisting toward his ribs. They spun into the brick wall. Dunne’s shoulder slammed Mace’s chest; breath left him in a grunt. The blade flashed past his cheek, close enough to feel the air move. Mace drove a knee into Dunne’s thigh, got a fistful of jacket, and they went down together, knees cracking against asphalt. The duffel tipped. Cash slid into a puddle.

Dunne bucked and clawed. Mace caught the knife wrist again, but his grip was wrong—slick, desperate. The blade turned in the scramble. He felt the point catch first as a sharp, cold pressure just below his ribs, like a knuckle pressed hard into muscle. Then Dunne shoved.

The cold broke into a tearing heat, thin and electric, as the blade went in and dragged sideways. Mace heard himself make a sound that wasn’t a word. His side went tight, then hot, then strangely numb, as if someone had poured warm water under his skin. The knife came free with a wet tug. Dunne scrambled backward, eyes wide, the blade shaking in his hand.

Mace pressed his palm to his side. Blood welled between his fingers, hot and slippery, startlingly fast. His breath came in short, shallow pulls; every inhale pulled at the wound like a hook. The alley tilted. The rain on his face felt far away. He tried to say something—something hard, something final—but all that came out was a thin, wet cough. Rain needled the alley behind the shuttered laundromat. Mace kept one hand on the duffel, the other loose near his coat pocket. Dunne stood too close, breath sour with cheap gin, counting the cash twice as if the second count might change the number.

“It’s short,” Dunne said.

“It’s not short. You said five for the whole box.”

“I said five if it was clean.”

Mace’s jaw tightened. “It’s clean.”

Dunne smiled without warmth. “Then open it.”

The box sat between them on a warped milk crate. Mace didn’t move. Dunne’s hand slipped into his jacket—not fast, almost lazy—and came out with a folding knife. The blade snicked open, a thin bright line in the wet dark.

“Don’t,” Mace said.

Dunne lunged anyway.

The first seconds were all elbows and wet gravel. Mace grabbed Dunne’s wrist with both hands, felt the tendons jumping under his grip, the knife hand twisting toward his ribs. They spun into the brick wall. Dunne’s shoulder slammed Mace’s chest; breath left him in a grunt. The blade flashed past his cheek, close enough to feel the air move. Mace drove a knee into Dunne’s thigh, got a fistful of jacket, and they went down together, knees cracking against asphalt. The duffel tipped. Cash slid into a puddle.

Dunne bucked and clawed. Mace caught the knife wrist again, but his grip was wrong—slick, desperate. The blade turned in the scramble. He felt the point catch first as a sharp, cold pressure just below his ribs, like a knuckle pressed hard into muscle. Then Dunne shoved.

The cold broke into a tearing heat, thin and electric, as the blade went in and dragged sideways. Mace heard himself make a sound that wasn’t a word. His side went tight, then hot, then strangely numb, as if someone had poured warm water under his skin. The knife came free with a wet tug. Dunne scrambled backward, eyes wide, the blade shaking in his hand.

Mace pressed his palm to his side. Blood welled between his fingers, hot and slippery, startlingly fast. His breath came in short, shallow pulls; every inhale pulled at the wound like a hook. The alley tilted. The rain on his face felt far away. He tried to say something—something hard, something final—but all that came out was a thin, wet cough. The call came in at 3:47 a.m. By the time Voss ducked under the tape, rain had washed the alley into a wet black throat between two brick buildings. The smell hit first—iron, urine, wet cardboard, the sweet rotten exhale of a dumpster. Under all of it, copper. A lot of copper.

The body lay half behind the dumpster, one arm flung out like he’d been reaching for something that wasn’t there. Male, white, thirties. Throat opened ear to ear. In the sodium light the blood wasn’t red; it was black and syrupy at the edges, pooling in an oil-slick rainbow on the cracked asphalt. Spray fanned up the brick wall in a low arc, and a handprint slid down through it, smeared at the bottom where the victim had tried to push himself upright.

Voss crouched. His knees popped. He breathed through his mouth, but the taste still got in—pennies and wet ash.

Left shoe missing. Belt undone. No wallet. A pale watch tan line on the wrist. Six, maybe seven knife wounds in the torso, clustered close and ugly, not random. One defensive slice across the left palm, deep enough to show the pale meat underneath. A fingernail torn back to the quick.

The medical examiner crouched opposite him, gloved fingers lifting the victim’s chin. Rain ticked off the dumpster lid.

“Time?” Voss asked.

“Two hours, maybe less. Throat cut first or near first. Torso wounds might be postmortem. Rain’s not helping.”

“Cut clean?”

“No. Two passes. Sawing at the end.”

Voss leaned in, studied the wound edges, the angle, the way the skin gaped. “Left-handed? Or standing over him?”

“Can’t say yet.”

Voss stood and scanned the ground. Drag marks from the middle of the alley to the dumpster—two parallel heel streaks in wet grit, blood diluted to pink. A cigarette butt under the victim’s shoulder, dry. Not his, maybe. Voss bagged it. Near the drain, a footprint, size eleven, tread worn at the heel. He photographed it. A uniform held back a kid on a bike at the mouth of the alley. Voss didn’t look at the kid. He looked at the wall. Low spray, then higher. Victim went down, got up, went down again. Or the killer knelt. He did the math. Five-eight, maybe. Right-handed, close. Angry. Personal.

He crouched again. The victim’s eyes were open, rain collecting in the sockets. Blue. Voss noted it, then looked away. He didn’t feel sorry. He felt the shape of the thing. The order of events. That was the job. The sorry came later, if it came.

“Any ID?” he asked.

“No wallet. No phone. Pockets empty except a lighter and a folded receipt from a bodega on Ninth. Time-stamped 1:12 a.m.”

“Two hours,” Voss said. “He bought something. Smoked. Met someone.”

The ME zipped the bag. “You want to wait for photos?”

“I want coffee,” Voss said. “But I’ll wait.”

He stepped back, listened to the rain drum the dumpster, the wet hiss of tires on the avenue. The alley smelled like a slaughterhouse drain. He wrote in his notebook: *Victim male, 30s. Throat cut, 6–7 stab wounds torso, defensive wound left palm. No wallet. Cigarette butt dry. Drag marks. Footprint 11. Possible left-handed killer? Check receipt. Bodega cam.*

Then he put the pen away, looked at the body one last time, and felt nothing but the small clean click of a fact fitting into place.

The blast did not end the market so much as erase its sound. One moment there had been the dense human noise of a crowded bazaar—vendors calling prices, carts rattling over stone, children threading between legs—and then a white flash, a concussive punch, and afterward a silence so total it felt like pressure against the ears.

Smoke drifted low through the stalls, gray and acrid, carrying the smell of scorched cloth, dust, and something sweeter and coppery beneath it. Awnings hung in torn strips. Fruit had been thrown from crates and lay bruised and bleeding in the dirt. A cart stood on its side, one wheel still spinning slowly, ticking as it turned. Shards of glass glittered everywhere, and paper and produce and scraps of clothing had been pasted to walls by the force of the blast.

The bodies were scattered where the crowd had been thickest. Some lay face down, arms flung out as if they had tried to push the ground away. Others were curled inward, knees drawn up. A woman sat slumped against a stall with her basket still looped over one arm, as though she had simply stopped in the middle of a sentence. Nearby, a man’s hand lay open on the cobbles, palm up, fingers relaxed. A child’s sandal rested alone in the dust. The dead did not look asleep; they looked abruptly unfinished, caught in the middle of ordinary motion.

Around them, the injured began to move. A man coughed and tried to rise, then fell back. Someone moaned from beneath a collapsed awning. A woman’s voice rose in a thin, wordless cry, then broke. But these sounds seemed small and far away, swallowed by the strange hush. People who had been running a second before now stood still, staring, their faces gray with dust and shock. No one screamed at first. That was the worst part—the way the market held its breath, the way the silence seemed to wait, as if the world itself had not yet decided what had happened.

Then, slowly, the hush began to fracture: a shutter creaking, glass crunching under a foot, someone whispering a name. But for those first long seconds, the devastated market lay under its cloud of dust in a terrible, eerie quiet—the sound of everything that had just been taken away.

He called it “taxidermy” only when he was angry with himself. Most days he called it listening.

The newest guest was Mr. Vale, a man in a green coat who had made the mistake of asking too many questions about the house on Alder Street. He had been killed elsewhere—the house was for afterward—and now he lay on the steel table in the basement, still wearing one shoe, his face slack with an expression the collector had already begun to think of as unfinished.

The basement smelled of cedar, dust, and something sweetly chemical that he never named aloud. He put on his apron and washed his hands twice. Then he stood over Mr. Vale and apologized, because he had found that apologies made the work steadier.

He began by emptying him. Not savagely—he was not a butcher—but carefully, the way one empties a suitcase after a long trip. The parts that would betray the body were removed and wrapped and taken away. He did not think of them as organs. He thought of them as weather: the rain of blood, the tide of breath, the soft machinery that had made Mr. Vale complain about the cold. What remained was the shape of the man, and the shape was what mattered.

He built the armature first. Wire and wood, bent to hold the shoulders at the angle Mr. Vale had used when he argued—one side slightly forward, chin lifted. The collector worked from memory and from a photograph he had taken before the green coat had been ruined. He fitted the frame inside the empty cavity and tested the posture by stepping back. Too stiff. He adjusted the spine. Better. Mr. Vale looked as if he were about to say something he would regret.

Then came the packing. He used cedar shavings, dry and fragrant, and a preservative he mixed in the dark of the workroom, never writing the proportions down. He packed the hollows in layers, not too tight, until the body held its own weight. He did not call this stuffing. Stuffing was for birds. This was more like giving someone back a shape they had misplaced.

The face was the hardest part. He had learned to leave the face for last, when his hands were tired and honest. He set the jaw with small metal pins, closed the mouth into a neutral line, and stitched the seams with tiny, even stitches that ran along the scalp and down the back, where the coat would hide them. He painted the lips a shade closer to living than they had been. He had a tray of glass eyes, each pair labeled in pencil. Mr. Vale’s were gray-blue, and the collector had painted them from a photograph, adding a tiny red thread of vein at the corner. When he set them in place, the room seemed to lean closer.

He dressed Mr. Vale in the green coat, which he had cleaned and pressed. He combed the hair. He dusted powder over the cheeks. Then he carried him upstairs—carefully, with both arms, the way one carries a sleeping child—and set him in the parlor chair by the window, facing the empty street. The other guests were already there: the woman in the blue dress, the man with the pipe, the boy who had sold newspapers and never stopped looking surprised. They sat in a loose semicircle, angled toward the window, as if waiting for a bus that was very late.

The collector stepped back and waited for the familiar feeling. Usually it came then: a quiet satisfaction, a sense that the house was full and no one was asking questions. But Mr. Vale’s mouth had shifted. Just slightly. The neutral line had become a smirk. The collector frowned, fetched his kit, and tightened the stitches. He turned Mr. Vale’s head a degree to the left. He adjusted the green coat. The smirk remained.

That night, he sat across from the collection and spoke to them. He told them about the mail, the neighbors, the price of coffee. He told them he was sorry. He told them they were the only company he could trust. The house settled around him, creaking in its old bones, and for a moment he thought he heard the soft rustle of fabric, as if someone had shifted in their chair.

He told himself it was the wind. He told himself the guests were quiet. But when he went to the basement to clean his tools, he left the parlor door open, and he did not look back at Mr. Vale’s gray-blue eyes.

The following evening, a neighbor knocked. The collector answered with a smile and a lie. Behind him, in the parlor, the guests sat in their semicircle, dust settling on their lashes, and Mr. Vale’s mouth was still not quite closed.

The whip spoke before it struck. It made a thin, rising whistle as it cut the air, then a flat, brutal crack that seemed to come from everywhere at once. The prisoner flinched before the pain arrived, shoulders already braced against the post, breath held in a tight knot.

Then the leather landed.

The sound of the lash against his back was not a clean slap. It was wet and heavy, a dull, meaty thud with a sharp edge, like a rope striking a side of raw wood. For half a second there was only that impact, the shock of it travelling through him in a silent shudder. Then the skin tore.

It was a small, terrible sound—a wet split, like stiff cloth ripping along a seam, followed by a soft, sucking give as the braided tip dragged through. The flesh opened in a line, and blood welled up fast, bright and startled, beading along the wound before it broke and ran in a thin thread down his ribs.

The prisoner gasped, not loudly, as if the air had been knocked out of some deeper place than his lungs. His fingers curled against the post. The guard counted. The whip whistled again.

**THE QUIET PART**

**INT. WINDOWLESS OFFICE — NIGHT**

A bare room. Metal desk. Two chairs. A single manila folder. MARLOW, 50s, sits with the calm of an accountant. THE CLIENT, 40s, keeps their coat on.

**MARLOW**  
You’ve seen the sample reel. Three minutes. No cuts after the first minute. Sound is clean. That’s the product.

**CLIENT**  
I need exclusivity.

**MARLOW**  
Region-locked. One master, one duplicate for escrow. No digital. If it touches a server, it’s not ours anymore.

**CLIENT**  
How long from order to delivery?

**MARLOW**  
Fourteen days. Seven if you waive the background package. The asset is sourced, held, and prepped. We don’t rush the final sequence. Rushed work looks rushed.

**CLIENT**  
I don’t want a performance.

**MARLOW**  
You won’t get one. We don’t coach. We don’t script. We frame and we roll. The room is controlled. The lighting is flat. The audio is primary. You said you wanted it to feel like evidence, not cinema.

**CLIENT**  
I said I wanted it to feel real.

**MARLOW**  
Then don’t ask for a soundtrack.

The Client opens the folder. Inside: a single sheet with checkboxes.

**CLIENT**  
Customization?

**MARLOW**  
Duration. Framing. Whether the face is visible. You cannot specify methods. That’s our department. It keeps the product consistent and the liability contained.

**CLIENT**  
Liability.

**MARLOW**  
Operational word. Not moral.

**CLIENT**  
Price.

**MARLOW**  
Fifty. Half on approval of the asset, half on delivery. Cash or equivalent. Courier fee separate. If you cancel after sourcing, the first half is forfeited. Sourcing is the expensive part.

**CLIENT**  
What if I don’t like it?

**MARLOW**  
You approve the asset before we roll. After that, you own the outcome. We don’t do refunds on finished product.

**CLIENT**  
And the asset?

**MARLOW**  
Not your concern. We handle disposal. You handle possession. You don’t ask where. You don’t ask who. You don’t call after delivery unless the media fails.

**CLIENT**  
If it fails?

**MARLOW**  
You return it. We replace the file. Same content, new master. No conversation.

**CLIENT**  
I want a guarantee there’s no copy.

**MARLOW**  
There’s no guarantee in this world. There’s procedure. One camera. One operator. One editor. The editor doesn’t know the source. The operator doesn’t know the buyer. You don’t know the operator. That’s the guarantee.

**CLIENT**  
You’re very calm.

**MARLOW**  
I’m at work.

**CLIENT**  
Do you watch them?

**MARLOW**  
Quality control. Beginning, middle, end. Sound sync. Exposure. Nothing else.

**CLIENT**  
Nothing else.

**MARLOW**  
I don’t have a personal interest in the product. I have an interest in repeat business.

**CLIENT**  
Will there be repeat business?

**MARLOW**  
That depends on whether you understand the terms. You’re buying a record. Not an experience. Not a relationship. Not a confession. A record. You take it home. You keep it private. You don’t contact me again unless you want another record.

**CLIENT**  
And if I do?

**MARLOW**  
Then we start again. New asset. New terms. Same discretion.

**CLIENT**  
The sample was… effective.

**MARLOW**  
That’s the word we use. Effective. It’s a better word than good.

**CLIENT**  
I’ll take the fourteen-day package.

**MARLOW**  
Then we’re in business. Leave the deposit with the man at the door. Don’t bring a phone next time.

**CLIENT**  
Next time?

**MARLOW**  
There’s always a next time. That’s not optimism. It’s inventory.

Marlow closes the folder. The Client stands. Neither offers a hand.

**The First Bite**

On the ninth day, the mountain made a sound like a house settling. It was only the wind scraping the fuselage, but Nia woke with her heart going, certain someone had spoken. The cabin smelled of frost, fuel, and the sweetness of unwashed bodies. Outside, the snow was a white blindness. Inside, Tomas lay under the emergency blanket, his face covered by the sleeve of his own coat.

They had stopped saying his name the night before. That was the first crack, though Nia did not recognize it then. They spoke of “him” and “the body” in the same low voice people use in church. Garret had made a rule: no one talks about it until everyone agrees. No one agreed. No one disagreed. The silence did the work.

Nia’s hunger had stopped being hunger days ago. It had become a hand inside her, clenching and unclenching. She dreamed of bread and woke with her jaw sore from chewing snow. The others slept in a huddle near the tail. She was supposed to be watching the weak light for planes. Instead she watched the blanket.

She tried to pray and heard herself thinking, *He is dead. I am not.* The thought arrived so plainly that she looked around, as if someone else had said it.

She crawled across the aisle. Her knees made no sound. The cold had taken the smell away, which was a mercy she did not feel she deserved. She lifted the edge of the blanket and saw Tomas’s hand, gray as candle wax, the wedding ring loose on the third finger. She remembered him laughing on the second day, telling a stupid story about a dog he’d had as a boy. The memory was so clear it seemed obscene. She put the blanket back.

Then the hand inside her clenched, and she doubled over, dry-heaving nothing.

When she could breathe again, she understood that the barrier was not disgust. Disgust was easy. The barrier was the story she had been telling herself about who she was. A person who did not do this. A person whose love for the dead was stronger than her fear of dying. The story had held for nine days. It was thinner now than the blanket.

She did not decide. That was the thing she would try to explain later and fail. She noticed she had already decided. She had the shard of plexiglass under her cuff. She had been carrying it for two days without admitting why. Her hands were steady. That steadiness frightened her more than the act itself.

“I’m sorry,” she whispered.

The apology was the last door. If he could hear her, then he was still there, and she could not do it. So she made him not there. She took his name and set it outside herself, carefully, like a coat she would never wear again. What remained was a body. Cold. Dead. Protein. A thing that had been loved and was now a problem of survival.

She cut a narrow strip from his forearm. The plexiglass was dull and sawed rather than sliced. Her stomach turned, but her hands kept moving. She thought of the butcher’s shop near her apartment, the clean white paper, the red meat behind glass. She thought of anything but Tomas. When the piece came free, she held it in her palm and waited to be struck by lightning.

Nothing happened. The wind scraped the fuselage. Someone coughed in their sleep.

She put it in her mouth.

It was cold first, then salt and iron, and something wrong that had no name. It tasted like biting her own tongue. Her body knew before her mind did, and her throat closed. She gagged, spat it into her hand, and sat shaking. For a moment she thought she had won. She was still a person. She could starve as a person.

Then the hand inside her clenched again, and she was so hungry that the world narrowed to a white point. She put the piece back in her mouth and chewed. It took a long time. She swallowed.

The first swallow was the break. Not the cut, not the taste. The swallow. She felt it go down and become part of her, and she waited for the shame to burn her clean. Instead she felt a small, animal quiet. Her body had accepted what her mind was still screaming about.

She wept without sound, one hand pressed to her mouth. Then she cut a second piece, smaller, because the first had not killed her. She chewed and swallowed and hated herself in a way that was almost peaceful. Behind her, Garret stirred under the blankets. Nia hid the shard and wiped her mouth with snow. Her hands were still steady.

That was what she would remember. Not the taste. Not the prayer. The steadiness.
